opus-5.5.text:
Well, the fundamental issue is that if you look at how AI models are actually structured, they're naturally dataflow graphs. You've got a sequence of operators — matrix multiplies, attention, normalizations, activations — and data flows from one to the next. The traditional way of executing that on a GPU is kernel by kernel: you launch a kernel, it reads its inputs from off-chip memory, does its computation, writes the results back out to HBM, and then the next kernel launches and reads them back in. Every one of those boundaries is a synchronization point, and it's a round trip to memory.

For inference in particular, and especially for the decode phase of large language models, that's a real problem, because you're often memory-bandwidth bound. You're not limited by how many flops you have; you're limited by how fast you can move weights and activations. So if you're spending your time bouncing intermediate results back and forth to HBM and waiting on kernel launch overheads, a lot of your compute is just sitting idle.

What asynchronous dataflow lets you do is take that graph and map it spatially onto the hardware, so the operators are pipelined. Different parts of the chip are working on different stages of the computation at the same time, and data streams directly from one stage to the next through on-chip memory and the interconnect. Each unit fires when its inputs are ready — you don't need a global barrier that says "everybody stop, we're done with this layer." That's the asynchronous part, and it's important because the work in these models isn't perfectly balanced. If you force everything into lockstep, the fastest units wait for the slowest. With dataflow, you decouple them, you use buffering between stages, and you absorb that variability.

The other piece is fusion. When you can fuse many operators together — in some cases whole decoder layers — you keep the intermediate data on chip, you dramatically cut memory traffic, and you get much higher utilization of both compute and bandwidth. That's what lets you deliver very high tokens per second per user, which is increasingly what matters as people move to agentic workflows where one request fans out into many model calls and latency compounds.

And finally, it gives you flexibility. Models keep changing — mixture of experts, different attention variants, long context. A reconfigurable dataflow architecture lets the compiler restructure the pipeline for each model rather than baking one execution pattern into the hardware. So for me, it's really about matching the execution model of the hardware to the natural structure of the computation, and when you do that, you keep the machine busy doing useful work instead of waiting.

r001.rationale: The response identifies memory bandwidth and weight movement as inference constraints, but it does not mention the KV cache.

r002.rationale: It describes operators running in parallel and data moving through on-chip memory and an interconnect, but does not describe overlapping HBM access, computation, and communication between RDUs.

r003.rationale: It says asynchronous dataflow can keep the machine busy and contrasts this with GPU execution, but does not attribute higher GPU-relative utilization to RDUs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the fundamental problem with inference, and really with all these large models, is that you're trying to keep a lot of compute units fed, and the traditional way of doing that, the GPU way, is that you have a kernel-by-kernel execution model. You load the data, you run a kernel, you write the results back out to memory, you launch the next kernel, and so on. And the issue is that between those kernels you have these bubbles. The hardware is sitting idle while you're waiting on memory, or waiting for synchronization, or waiting for the host to launch the next thing. For training that's somewhat tolerable because you can batch things up and amortize it, but for inference, especially the decode phase, where you're generating one token at a time and the batch sizes are small, those bubbles really dominate. You can end up with utilization in the low single digits on very expensive silicon.

So the way we think about it, going back to the work we did at Stanford on Plasticine and then at SambaNova, is that a neural network is really a dataflow graph. It's a graph of operators with data dependencies between them. And if you map that graph spatially onto the chip, so that the output of one operator flows directly into the input of the next one through on-chip memory rather than going out to HBM and back, then the natural execution model is asynchronous. Each unit just fires when its inputs are available. There's no global clock, no global barrier, no one saying "everybody stop, now we'll do matmul number seventeen." The data itself drives the schedule.

And that does two things for you. First, it eliminates most of that synchronization overhead, because you've replaced control-flow synchronization with data-flow synchronization, which is much finer grained and much cheaper. Second, it lets you pipeline across layers. While one part of the chip is working on the attention for a given token, another part can already be doing the MLP for the previous one. So you get this streaming behavior where the compute is continuously busy and the memory system is continuously busy, instead of alternating between the two.

The other thing I'd say is that asynchrony is really what gives you tolerance to variability. In a real inference system you've got variable sequence lengths, you've got requests arriving at different times, you've got memory latencies that aren't deterministic. A synchronous bulk-synchronous model has to plan for the worst case, so you're always waiting for the slowest thing. An asynchronous dataflow model just absorbs that. If one operator is slow, the things that don't depend on it keep going. That's the key reason we've gone this way: it's the execution model that most closely matches what the computation actually is, and so it's the one that lets you keep the hardware busy without heroic efforts from the compiler or the programmer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses memory waits and HBM generally, but does not identify HBM bandwidth for model parameters and the KV cache as the inference bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes continuously busy compute and memory and on-chip dataflow, but does not describe overlapping RDU computation, HBM access, and communication between RDUs.

r003.rationale: It links asynchronous dataflow to keeping hardware busy, but does not identify RDUs or attribute higher RDU utilization relative to GPUs to that execution model.

astra-6.text:
The key is that you want work to execute as soon as its inputs are available. With asynchronous dataflow, an operation doesn’t have to wait for a global schedule to advance or for unrelated work to finish. It can consume its inputs, compute, and pass its results downstream.

That lets you overlap different parts of inference. While one part of the machine is moving data, another can be computing, and another can be processing the next input. If you have enough independent work and buffering, you can absorb variations in latency instead of letting them stall the whole machine.

It doesn’t eliminate bottlenecks—you still need sufficient memory bandwidth and a good mapping of the computation—but it gives you a way to keep the hardware doing useful work without forcing everything to move in lockstep.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the idea is to let computation happen as soon as the data it needs is available. You don’t want one part of the machine sitting idle just because another part hasn’t finished, or because you’re waiting at a global synchronization point.

In an asynchronous dataflow system, an operator can execute when its inputs arrive and there’s room for its output. That lets different stages overlap: one stage can be working on one input while the next stage is processing an earlier input. And if something slows down, backpressure controls the flow.

For inference, that gives you a way to exploit parallelism across the model while keeping intermediate data close to the computation. You’re spending less time moving data back and forth to memory and more time doing useful work. The goal is to keep the whole pipeline productive, rather than just making an individual arithmetic unit fast.
